nodes.text: @gadboit @ClearThinker66 @gerdosi Not sure about that. We got a nasty cold/cough last year. Also most of my life I didn’t get (symptomatic) colds and never had flu except in 2009 the mini pandemic. Had it for 3 days. I don’t need lots of head colds and URI’s to stay healthy 😬😬😬.

nodes.text: @jillneimark @ClearThinker66 @gerdosi ... if you have had 20y worth of antigenic drift since you last saw it.

nodes.author: kellywind
nodes.text:
@gadboit @ClearThinker66 @gerdosi Maybe, but not necessarily. Neither 1977/78 nor 2009 were unusually bad flu years, you know? 

It's a funny old world like that sometimes.

nodes.author: ClearThinker66
nodes.text: @gadboit @jillneimark @gerdosi And as soon as the restrictions ended, people were dropping like flies (I don’t mean dying) with infections and wondering why that was happening. It was perfectly obvious to me.

nodes.author: ClearThinker66
nodes.text: @gadboit @jillneimark @gerdosi And people kept on getting repeated Covid vaccines which, to my understanding, meant that the immune system was ‘saturated’ for Covid and didn’t react to other things. Am I right about that? It’s what an immunology consultant friend told me.

nodes.author: gadboit
nodes.text: @ClearThinker66 @jillneimark @gerdosi Yes there is a thing called "T-cell attrition". Your memory pool is finite, so if you keep stuffing it with Covid memory, something else will be dropping out. Another factor I've wondered about is bystander activation of naive Ts. Any time you give your immune system a big...

nodes.author: gadboit
nodes.text: @ClearThinker66 @jillneimark @gerdosi ... kick in the face with a vaccine you burn a bunch of naive Ts (of which you essentially have a finite supply) including some that aren't specific to those antigens (this is "bystander" activation). If you're having vaccines much more often than you would be catching things...

nodes.author: gadboit
nodes.text: @ClearThinker66 @jillneimark @gerdosi ... anyway that might be compromising your ability to respond to new viruses in the future. All this is why you need trials that don't just look at flu (or Covid) but at all influenza-like illness. Why vaccinate repeatedly for just 2 out of the ~200 viruses that cause the same...

nodes.author: gadboit
nodes.text: @ClearThinker66 @jillneimark @gerdosi ... thing? There is scarce evidence that those two are particularly worse than the others, and your immune memory is finite.

nodes.author: kellywind
nodes.text: @gadboit @ClearThinker66 @gerdosi 5 years ago I would have agreed with you about flu, COVID (& RSV) not being particularly worse than the others, but I really think they are now. Something I saw a few years ago completely convinced me that over 50% of the "influenza & pneumonia" deaths really were/are from them.

nodes.author: gadboit
nodes.text: @kellywind @ClearThinker66 @gerdosi It's very hard to find actual evidence that even influenza is worse. If you look on pubmed you find lots of papers saying everything else, even rhinoviruses, are actually worse than we thought. There's kind of a myth around flu because of 1918. But that was too long ago to...

nodes.author: gerdosi
nodes.text: @gadboit @kellywind @ClearThinker66 Yes, the only factors that are consistently linked to outcomes are health/immune status. Which in turn depends on metabolic and nutritional status, in this case including vitamin D.

nodes.author: kellywind
nodes.text:
@gerdosi @gadboit @ClearThinker66 No, ebola, rabies, and HIV are inherently more severe than flu. Measles is deadlier than chickenpox. 

Some viruses have a naturally higher IFR than others regardless of host factors.

nodes.author: gadboit
nodes.text: @kellywind @gerdosi @ClearThinker66 Ofc but I mean comparing typical respiratory viruses.

nodes.author: gadboit
nodes.text: @kellywind @ClearThinker66 @gerdosi ... have a super-accurate idea of what actually happened. And of course the virus was relatively novel, which always makes them more severe. So it's very hard to get a like-for-like comparison. Need a big trial with PCR tests to see what the real differences are now.

nodes.author: kellywind
nodes.text:
@gadboit @ClearThinker66 @gerdosi I wouldn't be surprised if 1918 was multiple co-occurring pandemics. 
I think "novelty = severity" is overblown. Ebola's severity is from intrinsic virulence factors, not so much pure novelty, and 2009 H1N1 was "inherently" milder than the 90 yo one it knocked out of existence.

nodes.author: gadboit
nodes.text: @kellywind @ClearThinker66 @gerdosi Yes for Ebola. But for Covid I think it was novelty.

nodes.text: @gadboit @ClearThinker66 @gerdosi I agree that evidence has been & remains lacking, but I was patchworking together various data sources towards the end of the pandemic, after everything was opened up, expecting "proof" that flu was only about 20% or so of adult P&1 mortality, and was shocked to see it was >50%.

nodes.author: kellywind
nodes.text: @gadboit @ClearThinker66 @gerdosi I don't expect you to just take my word for it, tho. Maybe I'll get bored at some point and look everything up again and write up a substack on it.
